div.p: This article examines whether localized clusters of similar industries produce agglomeration economies in the formal and informal sectors. We develop a Bayesian method to estimate a spatial autoregressive model with an endogenous independent variable. We use establishment-level census data that cover both formal registered and informal unregistered establishments in Cambodia. We find that the density of local employment has a significantly positive effect on productivity in the informal sector, but little effect in the formal sector. For manufacturing, a doubling of employment density increases productivity in the informal sector by 9% through local linkages and by 19% through spatial multiplier linkages, leading to a 28% increase in total. A spatial network magnifies the local impact of agglomeration economies in the informal sector.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: A spatial concentration of industrial production has crucial implications for developing economies. Firms and workers in an agglomerated area can benefit from agglomeration externalities through efficient sharing of local suppliers, better matching between employers and workers and knowledge spillovers (Duranton and Puga, 2004). Limited resources such as capital, human capital and infrastructure can be most efficiently utilized in an agglomerated area. Consequently, industrial agglomeration can promote economic growth at an early stage of development (Williamson, 1965;Fujita and Thisse, 2003).

However, it is an unsettled question as to whether industrial agglomeration produces similar benefits for low-income economies, as has been previously demonstrated for high-and middle-income countries (Rosenthal and Strange, 2004;Melo et al., 2009). In developing economies, self-employment and small enterprises provide major employment opportunities, but often do not formally register with the government. These informal enterprises are less productive and profitable than formally registered enterprises (McKenzie and Seynabou Sakho, 2010;Fajnzylber et al., 2011). Given the coexistence of formal and informal firms, Annez and Buckely (2009, 15) state that 'some critics argue that informality is unproductive and raises the costs to the formal sector, crowding out agglomeration economies'. In contrast, Overman and Venables (2005, 20) suggest that 'the informal sector also contributes to agglomeration economies'. Glaeser and Henderson (2017, 3) argue that agglomeration economies are important for informal firms that rely on trust and face-to-face interactions. Therefore, it is a crucial empirical question as to whether industrial agglomeration produces productivity gains in both formal and informal sectors.

In this article, we estimate the long-run magnitude of agglomeration economies produced by a localized concentration of similar industries in Cambodia-a developing economy with the large informal sector. A localized cluster of similar industries, as defined by similar industrial codes, can produce both positive externalities and congestion costs for producers. If positive externalities exceed congestion costs, regional productivity should increase with the density of local employment in similar industries, and vice versa. Moreover, industrial clusters form a spatial network among firms and workers through the spatial diffusion of agglomeration externalities. The spatial interdependence of productivity may magnify the local impact of localization economies through a spatial multiplier effect. Additionally, producers in the formal and informal sectors may benefit differently from agglomeration economies. Formal firms adopt modern production technology to produce high-quality products and services for high-income customers, whereas informal firms use traditional production technology to produce low-quality products and services for low income customers. Formal and informal firms may have weak linkages in production and technology, so that the formal and informal sectors are segregated in developing economies (La Porta and Shleifer, 2014). The segregation between the formal and informal sectors suggests that formal and informal firms may benefit differently from a localized concentration of similar industries in which formal and informal firms exist unevenly across regions.

We specify a spatial autoregressive model with an endogenous independent variable to identify the causal effect of localization economies in the formal and informal sectors. We address an endogeneity problem in agglomeration by exploiting past data on the density of local employment and forest area as instruments for the current density of local employment. We account for a spatial network among firms by a spatial lag variable of productivity, which allows us to estimate local and spatial magnitudes of localization economies. To estimate our model, we develop a Bayesian method by extending the Bayesian instrumental variables (IV) method proposed by Rossi et al. (2005).

We exploit a unique dataset based on the Economic Census of Cambodia in 2011 (EC2011). This census covers all nonfarm establishments across all industrial sectors in all areas of Cambodia and asks whether individual establishments are registered with the Ministry of Commerce. Unregistered economic activity is a commonly used definition of informality, and business registration is an objective criterion to classify formal and informal economic activities (Schneider and Enste, 2013). The dataset allows us to estimate agglomeration economies in both formal and informal sectors. Additionally, Cambodia provides an interesting setting for our analysis. The Cambodian economy was devastated by the Pol Pot regime for [1975][1976][1977][1978][1979] and the subsequent civil war. The Paris Conference on Cambodia in 1991 led to agreements on the comprehensive political settlement of the Cambodian conflict. While the economy experienced a rapid economic growth thereafter, per capita GDP reached only 931.2 USD in 2012 (IMF, 2012). Schneider et al. (2010) estimate that informal activity accounted for 48.7% of GDP in Cambodia on average for the period 1999-2007.

The main findings can be summarized as follows. The density of local employment has a significantly positive effect on productivity in the informal sector. Since the validity of our instruments is supported, we interpret the positive coefficient of employment density as reflecting a causal effect. In contrast, we find little evidence of localization economies in the formal sector. These contrasting results are found in both manufacturing and wholesale/retail industries. Additionally, a spatial lag of productivity is significantly positive in the informal sector, suggesting that the positive spatial interdependence magnifies the positive localization effects. Based on the main result for manufacturing, we find that a doubling of the density of local employment in a region increases productivity in the informal sector by 9% through direct linkages and by 19% through spatial multiplier linkages, leading to a 28% increase in total. As the spatial multiplier linkages magnify the local agglomeration effect substantially, the spatial network is crucial for estimating the precise magnitude of localization economies.

This article contributes to the related literature in several ways. Livingstone (1991) documents a spatial concentration of manufacturing microenterprises in developing economies, which are interpreted as evidence of externalities perceived by small producers. Drawing on case studies on industrial clusters, Schmitz (1995) and Schmitz and Nadvi (1999) examine how clustering promotes the growth and competitiveness of small manufacturers. In addition to local external economies from clustering in Marshall (1890), these papers highlight active joint action among firms in clusters. From a historical perspective, Zeitlin (2008) and Hashino and Otsuka (2013) explore long-term processes of industrial clusters and emphasize cooperative efforts among producers and local governments in clusters. On the other hand, Moreno-Monroy (2012) argues that small enterprises also exist in non-cluster areas and the case studies on successful industrial clusters may represent exceptions to the usual experience of small enterprises. In this respect, our article is advantageous in that we employ a comprehensive dataset on formal and informal firms to provide systematic evidence of clustering benefits.

A formal econometric approach has been taken to estimate agglomeration economies in developing economies, but informal enterprises are largely missed in prior analysis (Combes and Gobillon, 2015). 1 Duranton (2009, 82) argues that most of the econometric findings on agglomeration economies concern the formal sector. To fill this gap, recent studies attempt to estimate agglomeration economies in the informal sector. Chhair and Newman (2014) use the same dataset in Cambodia as our analysis and show a negative effect of agglomeration on productivity for registered and unregistered firms mainly through a competition channel. However, they do not fully address an endogeneity issue of clustering, thereby showing only correlation relationships. Ali and Peerings (2011) address an endogeneity issue in agglomeration by matching firms with similar characteristics between clustered and dispersed areas. In the handloom sector in Ethiopia, they find larger monthly profits for clustered small firms than non-clustered small. As clustering is defined by a cut-off point of the location quotient, they find that an increase in the cut-off point leads to higher profits for clustered firms, making their estimates sensitive to the definition of clustering. Additionally, Garcı´a (2016) use Colombian worker-level surveys to estimate a relationship between employment density and wages for informal workers, who are not covered by the healthcare insurance and the retirement pension. The results show that the density increases wages for informal workers, but decreases for formal workers. While endogeneity of density is addressed by an instrumental-variables method, a large number of informal workers such as unpaid family workers may be missed in the survey data, suggesting that the coverage of informal workers is limited.

Compared with these prior studies, our paper is distinctive in that employment density is measured by all workers in formal registered and informal unregistered establishments. The establishment-level census data allow us to measure density of employment, including self-employed proprietors, unpaid family workers, and regular employees. The comprehensive coverage of the formal and informal sectors is a unique feature of our study because informal activities are often missed in official statistics in developing economies. Moreover, we exploit systematic empirical data on labor density and geographic characteristics in the past period as instruments to identify a causal effect of local employment density on productivity in both formal and informal sectors. As our measure of agglomeration does not rely on a specific measurement of clustering, we provide a robust estimate of agglomeration effects on productivity.

A spatial econometric model has been applied to estimate agglomeration economies. Van Oort (2007) adopts a feasible generalized least squares method to estimate the impact of industrial concentration on industrial employment growth in the Netherlands. The spatial lag of industrial concentration is included to capture agglomeration effects in neighboring regions, which are found to increase employment growth. Ke (2010) estimates a simultaneous equation model of industrial output and non-agricultural labor productivity for city-level data in mainland China. After accounting for labor productivity in neighboring cities, a spatial concentration of industrial production is found to increase the productivity. Additionally, Artis et al. (2012) adopt a feasible generalized spatial two-stage least-squares method proposed by Kelejian and Prucha (1998) to account for both endogeneity of agglomeration and regional productivity in neighboring regions. Using regional data in the UK, they find a positive impact of agglomeration on productivity. Consistent with these studies, we find that agglomeration increases productivity in the same region after accounting for spatial externalities across regions. In contrast, we further demonstrate that a spatial network magnifies substantially the local impact of agglomeration economies through spatial multiplier linkages.

Finally, we make a methodological contribution to this line of inquiry. A Bayesian approach to instrumental variables regression has long been developed since the work of Dre`ze (1976). It is increasingly used to estimate a spatial autoregressive model (Banerjee et al., 2004;LeSage and Pace, 2009). Extending prior methods, we apply a Bayesian method for a spatial autoregressive model with an endogenous independent variable. To estimate such a model, Kelejian and Prucha (1998) propose higher order spatial lags of exogenous independent variables as instruments for the spatial lag of a dependent variable. However, Gibbons and Overman (2012) argue that this approach suffers from estimation problems for identification because the higher order spatial lags are assumed to have no direct influence on the dependent variable, and these instruments may be weak because of potentially high correlations among the higher order spatial lags. In contrast, our Bayesian approach does not exploit the higher order spatial lags as instruments, thereby relaxing the identification assumptions used in the prior method. Additionally, it should be mentioned that Hashiguchi and Tanaka (2014) develop a Bayesian method for a hierarchical spatial model at the firm-level to address both endogeneity of agglomeration and spatial autocorrelation at the regional level. Because spatial autocorrelation of productivity among individual firms are not estimated in their model, they do not calculate a potential spatial multiplier effect of agglomeration economies. In contrast, this article develops a spatial model to calculate the spatial multiplier.

Taken together, we contribute to the agglomeration literature by estimating agglomeration economies in formal and informal sectors. We address both the endogeneity of agglomeration and the spatial dependence of productivity to estimate local and spatial impacts of industrial clusters separately for formal and informal firms. We also contribute to the spatial econometric literature by developing a Bayesian method for a spatial autoregressive model with an endogenous independent variable. Thus, this article contributes by carrying out these extensions together.

The rest of this article is organized as follows. Section 2 discusses a conceptual framework. Section 3 presents a spatial autoregressive model with an endogenous independent variable. Section 4 explains the Bayesian method for estimating our empirical model. Section 5 describes the data sources and the structure of industrial activity in Cambodia. Section 6 presents the estimation results. Section 7 concludes.

div.head: Conceptual framework
div.p: The main objective of our analysis is to estimate the long-run magnitude of agglomeration economies produced by a localized concentration of similar industries in a developing economy where both formal and informal firms exist unevenly across regions but are largely segregated. In the literature, Schneider and Enste (2013, Chapter 2) define the national economy as the dual economy of official sector and underground sector, the latter of which consists of the shadow economy based on market transactions and the household sector based on non-market transactions for selfsufficient individual needs. Our definition of the formal and informal sectors corresponds to the official sector and the shadow economy, respectively.

div.head: Agglomeration economies and spatial networks
div.p: To develop a conceptual framework, we start to discuss a concept of agglomeration economies and the network formation of firms and workers over space, followed by an argument of why the formal and informal sectors may benefit differently from agglomeration effects. As is well known, Marshall (1890) argues that a cluster of firms can be more productive for localization economies through specialized suppliers, labor market pooling and knowledge spillovers. Firms need specialized equipment and support services to produce and develop goods and services. A localized cluster of firms provides a large market for supporting the specialized suppliers, which in turn produce a wide range of inputs at a low cost for firms in a cluster. Additionally, a cluster of firms supports a large pool of workers with a variety of specialized skills. In a pooled labor market, there is better matching between employers and employees, which reduces labor shortages and unemployment, respectively. Finally, knowledge and technology are crucial inputs of production. An exchange of information and knowledge takes place through personal Agglomeration economies . 41 interactions, and knowledge spillovers benefit producers and workers more effectively in a clustered area. In sum, firms and workers in a cluster benefit from localization externalities through more efficient sharing of local suppliers, better matching between employers and workers, and knowledge spillovers (Duranton and Puga, 2004).

These discussions suggest that a localized cluster of similar industries can produce positive externalities for producers. On the other hand, a spatial concentration of firms and workers increases congestion costs from congested roads, higher land prices and environmental pollution. Industrial clusters produce not only localization economies, but also congestion costs to reduce producers' productivity in a clustered area. Thus, if positive externalities exceed congestion costs, regional productivity should increase with the density of local employment in similar industries, and vice versa. Our first hypothesis is as follows.
Hypothesis 1. Regional productivity would be higher in regions with a greater density of local employment in similar industries if localization economies exceed congestion effects.

Formation of industrial clusters depends on local natural advantages, including geography, natural resources, economic infrastructure and social institutions. Some regions with strong natural advantages attract firms and workers, and vice versa. In addition, the spatial diffusion of knowledge externalities in a cluster shapes the network formation of firms and workers over space. Firms and workers in neighboring areas benefit from localization economies through spatial interactions with firms and workers in a clustered area. However, such spatial externalities decay as distance increases because the costs of economic and social interactions increase over space and deter the diffusion of knowledge across greater distances. Consequently, industrial clusters shape the spatial network among firms and workers, leading to the spatial interdependence of economic performance. Our second hypothesis is the following.

Hypothesis 2. Regional productivity would have a positive spatial interdependence if the spatial diffusion of positive knowledge externalities shapes the network formation of firms and workers over space.

div.head: Segregation between formal and informal firms
div.p: A distinction between the formal and informal sectors is crucial for understanding localization economies in a developing economy. In the formal sector, highly educated entrepreneurs typically manage firms to produce high quality products and services for high income customers using modern production technology with skilled labor and large capital equipment. Formal firms register with the government to establish a legal entity, and register with the tax authority to pay formal taxes based on their balance sheets. In the informal sector, uneducated entrepreneurs typically manage firms to produce low-quality products and services for low-income customers using traditional production technology with unskilled labor and small capital equipment. Informal firms conduct business activities but do not formally register with the government and the tax authority. Since they buy and sell in cash, they often lack bank accounts and accounting books. A comparison of these sectors indicate that formal firms are more likely than informal firms to be more productive, more profitable and larger in size (La Porta and Shleifer, 2014).

As suggested in the dual view of informality by Lewis (1954), the formal and informal sectors in a developing economy are largely segregated. Formal (informal) firms have more intensive relationships with other formal (informal) firms, although these sectors may not be completely isolated from each other. The segregation may arise from the weak technological and production linkages between these sectors. Formal firms typically build modern manufacturing facilities to expand production capacity and improve the quality of products. As technical and managerial skills are required to implement modern production systems, they adopt structured management practices such as human resource management. Informal firms use traditional production methods with simple tools and equipment for small-scale production and thus do not require modern management practices. Such a large gap in technology and management practices implies that formal firms would not gain knowledge and technology spillovers from informal firms, whereas informal firms have limited capabilities to absorb the spillovers from formal firms.

The technology gap consequently restricts vertical linkages between formal and informal firms. Formal firms require suppliers to produce parts and components of high quality at a competitive price and to supply them at a low defection rate in timely delivery. Such high requirements for suppliers effectively limit the participation of most informal firms in value chains for the formal sector (Moreno-Monroy, 2012). The level of subcontracting from formal to informal firms is quite limited in developing countries partly because formal firms rely importantly on imported intermediate inputs (Lim, 1984;Arimah, 2001;Bo¨hme and Thiele, 2014). Additionally, vertical linkages between these sectors are discouraged by tax systems in developing countries. For instance, formally registered firms in Cambodia are required to register with the General Department of Taxation to obtain a value-added tax (VAT) identification number. These firms must charge VAT on their sales and issue VAT invoices that contain the VAT identification numbers of suppliers and buyers. With the proper VAT invoices, taxpayers can offset the VAT paid on their purchases against the VAT paid on their sales. Because the tax authority does not accept the VAT invoices without the VAT identification numbers, the registered firms cannot claim tax credits for their purchases from unregistered suppliers. On the other hand, unregistered firms do not have the VAT identification number and thus cannot claim the VAT credit.foot_2 Consequently, formal (informal) firms favor business transactions with other formal (informal) firms over those with informal (formal) firms. de Paula and Scheinkman (2010) show that the VAT system creates informality chains in Brazil.

Linkages between the formal and informal sectors are also limited by worker transitions between these sectors. As described to characterize labor market dualism, formal firms are more likely than informal firms to offer more attractive wages and employment benefits (Fields, 2009). While workers in the informal sector may seek a more attractive job in the formal sector, relatively high skill requirements and stringent work environment pose a barrier to informal workers who are typically uneducated and lack work experiences in a modern company. While transitions of workers between formal and informal sectors exist in both directions, prior studies show that most workers stay in either the formal or informal sector, suggesting the lower transitions between the formal and informal sectors (Maloney, 1999, McCaig andPavcnik, 2015;Meghir et al., 2015).

The segregation between the formal and informal sectors suggests that formal and informal firms may benefit differently from a localized concentration of similar industries in which formal and informal firms exist unevenly across regions. Formal firms may benefit strongly from a localized cluster of formal firms for strong networks and interactions, but weakly from that of informal firms for weak networks and interactions. On the other hand, informal firms may benefit strongly from a localized cluster of informal firms for strong social interactions through trust-based transactions and face-to-face contacts in neighborhood (Glaeser and Henderson, 2017). They benefit weakly from that of formal firms for weak interactions with formal firms. While the density of local employment should produce cluster benefits in the formal and informal sectors, the uneven existence of formal and informal firms in a localized cluster would produce varying cluster benefits. This implies that aggregating formal and informal firms may mask distinctive localization externalities. Thus, our third hypothesis is as follows.

Hypothesis 3. A greater density of local employment in similar industries would produce varying impacts on regional productivity in the formal and informal sectors if formal and informal firms coexist but are largely segregated for weak linkages in production and technology.

Our hypotheses suggest that a dense interaction among formal firms leads to the formation of spatial networks in the formal sector, which produces the spatial interdependence of economic performance in the formal sector. On the other hand, a strong interaction among informal firms produces spatial externalities in the informal sector, leading to the spatial dependence in the informal sector.

div.head: Mechanisms of agglomeration benefits for formal and informal firms
div.p: In this article, we aim to assess the overall net impact of localization economies on the formal and informal sectors, but do not seek to identify the underlying mechanisms of agglomeration gains and costs separately. 3 Nevertheless, it is useful to discuss plausible channels through which formal and informal firms benefit from a localized cluster of similar industries to help us interpret a regression analysis. Specifically, we focus on two related questions. (i) How differently do formal and informal firms benefit from agglomeration? (ii) What advantages do informal firms and workers in an industrial cluster have as compared to those in an isolated location?

In the first issue, we predict that informal firms would have larger agglomeration gains than formal firms. Formal firms typically adopt advanced production facilities and management practices. Production technology is often embodied in capital equipment, whereas managerial skills are embodied in experienced managers. The adoption of such technology and skills requires large investment in physical capital and human resources. On the other hand, informal firms typically adopt elementary production techniques to produce simple low-quality products. Such techniques can be learned and imitated through face-to-face interactions to produce similar products (Chung, 2012;Harris, 2014). Because more elementary technical knowledge is more easily absorbed and exploited, informal firms would benefit more strongly from knowledge spillovers in a cluster.

Formal firms can internalize a wide range of production and sales functions, including product design, in-house production of intermediate inputs, final assembly and distribution for sales. If in-house production of intermediate inputs is too costly, they can rely on imported raw materials and intermediate inputs, for which a local government in a developing country often provides only the formal sector with a preferential treatment such as tariff reduction and exemption system. The internalization allows formal firms to exploit increasing returns to scale. In contrast, informal firms tend to specialize in specific tasks for the inter-firm division of labor and survive by participating in value chains. They are dependent on local external economies generated by the participation of value chains (Schmitz, 1995). As they may be more dependent on local industries than formal firms, they would benefit more strongly from local production linkages in a cluster.

In the second issue, a starting point is to consider a business environment for informal firms in a developing country. As the legal protection and contract enforcement of informal businesses is weak, illegitimate activities such as fraud, nonrepayment, and petty theft are pervasive in the informal sector (Hart, 1973). Selfinterest of own profits may shape unequal business relations at the expense of partners, and thus market transactions are subject to the high risk of opportunistic behavior. To reduce high transaction costs, people have frequent face-to-face contacts and build trust among social and personal networks (Dijk and Rabellotti, 1997). Trust-based networks encourage the development of repeated transactions in the informal sector. Consequently, trust-based transactions allow for a deeper inter-firm relationship such as a provision of informal credit through subcontracting and sales of machinery and raw materials (Dei Ottati, 1994). Because spatial proximity facilitates face-to-face communication, clustered informal firms are advantageous in finding good partners in close proximity among a large pool of alternative partners and building trust-based transactions with good partners.

Social networks and long-term business transactions provide a basis for informal firms to benefit from Marshallian agglomeration benefits. In the case of knowledge spillovers, for example, Kimura (2011) studies the modernization process of a papermanufacturing village in Northern Vietnam from a traditional handicraft village into a modern industrial cluster. He shows that kinship networks help learning about the use of machine production technology and operational skills for mechanized production. The operation knowledge was diffused from one village pioneer to his sons and relatives, and subsequently to other followers in the village. Additionally, based on a qualitative study of the handicraft industry in Nairobi, Kenya, Harris (2014) finds that proximity to suppliers is crucial for the location decision of clustered informal firms because small-batch middlemen in a cluster provide better access to needed materials in the quantities demanded. From a buyer's point of view, a cluster of individual operators can collectively fill a product order of any significant size and variety through subcontracting to neighboring operators. As a result, clustered informal firms can benefit from a local pool of suppliers and customers. Finally, workers in the informal sector are often non-permanent employees such as casual laborers and face a high risk of unemployment. Information on job vacancies flow along social networks in the informal sector (Hart, 1973), while public employment offices play an insignificant role. Informal workers in a cluster can reduce the risk of unemployment and benefit from greater job opportunities for proximity to employers (Harris, 2014).

There are alternative channels such as informal finance through which informal firms benefit from clustering. 4 As a financial market in developing countries is underdeveloped, formal access to credit such as bank loans are limited for informal firms. An important source of funds is their own savings and credit through personal networks such as borrowing from family, friends and neighbors for mutual support. These financial resources are used for an initial capital investment to start a micro business (Bagachwa, 1997;Kimura, 2011). Meanwhile, the fine division of labor in an industrial cluster reduces an entry barrier for specific segments of production processes, thereby lowering the capital requirements for informal firms to enter an industry (Ruan and Zhang, 2009). Thus, clustered informal firms would be more likely than isolated firms to take advantage of informal finance to mitigate capital constraints.

div.p: where y s i and y s j are a measure of productivity in regions i and j, respectively. Regional productivity is measured by the log of total factor productivity (TFP) for region i and sector s. The variable w ij represents the degree of geographical connectivity between regions i and j in the following form:
div.formula: w ij ¼ 0 for i ¼ j d À1 ij P n j d À1 ij for i 6 ¼ j 8 > < > :
div.p: where d ij is travel time between regions i and j. The parameter is the magnitude of spatial autocorrelation in regional productivity. x i is a variable to capture agglomeration of similar industries in region i. z i is a vector of control variables, and " i is an error term.

We are interested in an estimate of the coefficient 0 , which represents the magnitude of net agglomeration effects arising from both localization economies and congestion effects in a localized cluster of similar industrial activities. Following the prior literature (Ciccone and Hall, 1996;Bru¨lhart and Mathys, 2008;Broersma and Oosterhaven, 2009), we measure industrial agglomeration by using the density of local employment in 4 Other clustering benefits for informal firms may include trade networks in which low search and reach costs in a cluster attract trading middlemen from other regions (Weijland, 1994;Sato, 2000). similar industries: ln Employment i =Area i ð Þ .foot_5 Thus, the coefficient 0 represents an elasticity of regional productivity with respect to the density of local employment. Since we exploit cross-regional variation in employment density, we interpret the estimated elasticity as indicating the net localization effects that have accumulated during past periods up to the point of the year in our cross-section data. 6In examining the formal and informal sectors, we distinguish between manufacturing and service industries because industrial clusters in these industries may produce agglomeration economies differently. A manufactured product can be physically transported from a production plant to a consumer at a distance. Meanwhile, services are often produced in person, making it important to produce services near a consumer. Such a characteristic of services gives an incentive for services industries to concentrate in urban areas. Kolko (2010) finds that manufacturing industries tend to be more agglomerated than service industries in the USA. As agglomeration benefits are likely to increase in more agglomerated industries, Graham (2009) shows that the elasticity of localization economies tends to differ in magnitude across manufacturing and service industries. While our aim is to estimate agglomeration economies in the formal and informal sectors, the analysis may be biased if only manufacturing industry is examined. Thus, we estimate the coefficient 0 separately for four subsamples of our dataset: formal manufacturing, informal manufacturing, formal services, and informal services.

Potential spatial interdependence in regional productivity is modeled as a spatial lag variable, P n j¼1 w ij y s j , which can be considered as arising from the network formation of firms and workers over space (Corrado and Fingleton, 2012). Conceptually, our approach is similar to the prior literature in that spatial spillovers in knowledge and technology are captured by the spatial lag variable of total factor productivity in regional production function (Ertur and Koch, 2007;Hashiguchi, 2010). From an econometric point of view, significant spatial autocorrelation may magnify or reduce the impact of local employment density through a spatial multiplier effect on productivity across regions. Thus, the spatial lag variable allows us to estimate the global magnitude of localization economies.

Our control variables are defined as follows. First, the local market size can affect both agglomeration and productivity. We control for the market size by the population size in region i. Second, Jacobs urbanization economies can raise productivity in regions with a more diverse range of different industrial activities. To control for cross-industry externalities, we define an industrial diversity index for industry k as:

More intensive competition encourages managerial efforts to improve productivity. Meanwhile, stronger competition decreases the market share of individual producers, and a decline in the scale of production reduces productivity. To account for local competition effects, we define a competition index as:

Regional productivity depends in part on industrial infrastructure such as access to electricity. We include an electricity access variable as measured by the proportion of households with access to city power or a generator for the main source of light in region i. Additionally, skilled workers may concentrate in denser areas, such as large cities, which contributes to spatial wage disparities (Glaeser and Mare´, 2001;Combes et al., 2008). Andersson et al. (2007) show that more productive workers are matched with more productive firms in a denser region through assortative matching and production complementarity. To control for the linkage between skilled workers and agglomeration, we include a high-skill variable as measured by the proportion of persons completing technical/vocational diplomas and undergraduate/graduate degrees in region i. On the other hand, unskilled workers may reside in dispersed areas with lower regional productivity. Thus, we include a low-skill variable as measured by the proportion of persons completing only primary and secondary school programs in region i.

div.head: Reduced form equation
div.p: We seek to identify the causal impact of localization economies on regional productivity after controlling for a variety of regional characteristics that may affect regional productivity. The inclusion of control variables z i helps to reduce an omitted-variables bias in the estimated coefficient of localization economies, 0 . However, some regions may be endowed with unobserved natural advantages such as local climate, social infrastructure and natural resources. If these natural advantages attract more skilled workers for higher wages, the estimated coefficient, 0 , may contain a bias. Additionally, more productive firms may self-select to locate their economic activity in agglomerated regions to benefit from positive externality. Unobserved heterogeneity in the location decisions by individual firms may cause a reverse-causality bias in the estimated coefficient, 0 . Thus, there is a concern about an endogeneity bias in the estimation of localization economies. 7To deal with the endogeneity problem, we employ the Bayesian instrumentalvariables method proposed by Rossi et al. (2005). We specify the reduced form equation:
div.formula: x i ¼ q i c 0 þ z i c 1 þ ið2Þ
div.p: where x i is an endogenous variable and assumed to be linearly related to a set of instruments q i ; z i À Á . q i is a vector of exogenous variables related to x i , but independent of the error term i . For instrumental variables, we exploit regional characteristics in a past period including the density of employment in similar industries and the geographic characteristics as measured by the share of forest and shrubland area. We use data in 1998 for employment and in 2002 for geography. The identifying assumption is that the employment density and geographic characteristics in the past period have persistent influences only on the preferences of workers about the location in which they seek employment opportunities. However, these instruments are not correlated with the current differences in regional productivity that are not explicitly accounted for by our model. Our approach follows Ciccone and Hall (1996) and Ciccone (2002) in that past labor and geography are used as instruments for current agglomeration.

Our instruments can be justified as follows. First, industrial agglomeration is a result of a cumulative process in which individual economic activities are attracted to specific points in geographic areas over time. A large concentration of economic activity in one region is more likely than a small concentration in another region to attract a larger number of workers because of the larger market size and wider availability of intermediate inputs and consumer products (Fujita et al., 1999). Consequently, the past density of labor should positively affect the formation of industrial agglomeration in specific regions. Additionally, we hypothesize that geographic characteristics affect the patterns of locations where workers seek jobs. Forest and shrubland regions are more likely than plain regions to deter the formation of industrial activity for the high cost of leveling the ground, thereby yielding a geographic barrier to worker settlement. Past land characteristics should negatively influence the formation of industrial agglomeration. Consistent with our justifications, Combes et al. (2010) emphasize the usefulness of history and geology as instruments of agglomeration.

Exclusion restrictions of our instruments imply that labor density and geographic characteristics in the past are assumed to affect current regional productivity only through the current level of industrial agglomeration, but should not affect the regional productivity through other channels that are not explicitly accounted for by control variables, z i . If our instruments produce unobserved persistent effects on a local market over time, they affect the contemporaneous determinants of regional productivity. As long as such persistent influences are captured by any of the control variables, the exclusion restrictions are satisfied. On the other hand, any remaining correlation between instruments and unobserved current shocks violates the exclusion restrictions. For instance, past density and geography might produce unobserved shocks to regional productivity in the past period, which remain to affect current productivity through cumulation effects. If such linkages are not sufficiently accounted for by the control variables, it may be difficult to give a causal interpretation for an estimate of localization economies.foot_8 Thus, we calculate the Sargan statistic to check the validity of the exclusion restrictions.

Finally, we emphasize that the recent economic growth of the Cambodian economy helps to meet the exclusion restrictions. The economy has experienced the rapid economic growth since the early 1990s, and its industrial structure has been substantially transformed from agriculture to manufacturing and services; for instance, the share of agriculture in GDP declined from 55.6% in 1990 to 33.8% in 2010, while the share of manufacturing increased from 5.2% to 14.9% during this period (Hill and Menon, 2013). These rapid structural changes should help to isolate our instruments based on past data from unobserved current shocks to regional productivity.

Through face-to-face interviews, the enumerators filled out a questionnaire for each establishment. The NIS collected all the questionnaires for data input and checked data consistency by comparing two data files that were made separately by two data-input operators.

In the EC2011 questionnaire, each establishment is asked whether or not they register with the Ministry of Commerce or the Provincial Department of Commerce. 12 In the registration process, formal firms must provide the registrar with the specific location of their office and the name of their agent. 13 The registration procedures require a firm (i) to deposit the legally required initial capital in a bank and obtain deposit evidence, (ii) conduct an initial check of the uniqueness of the company name at the Intellectual Property Department and the Business Registration Office, and (iii) publish an abstract of the company organization documents and incorporate the company with the Business Registration Department in the Ministry of Commerce (World Bank, 2014). These procedures are estimated to cost at least 400 USD and to take one month. For analysis, we exploit the registration question to define the formal sector as the business activities of registered firms and the informal sector as the activities of unregistered firms. Thus, the EC2011 provides a unique dataset to examine the entire coverage of the formal and informal sectors.

To gauge the relative importance of the shadow economy in Cambodia, Table 1 presents aggregate data on formal and informal establishments, with the financial figures measured for one month in February 2011. Across all industries, there were 17, 374 formal establishments and 487, 719 informal establishments. 14 The informal sector represents 96.6% of the total number of establishments, 76.6% of total sales, 59.2% of total wages and 66.4% of total employment. For manufacturing industries, there were 1723 formal establishments and 69,693 informal establishments, with the informal sector representing 97.6% of firms, 60.8% of sales, 35.8% of wages and 32.5% of employment. On the other hand, there were 6245 formal establishments and 286,101 informal establishments in wholesale and retail trade industries, with the informal 10 In preparing for the EC2011, the NIS made the establishment listing in Phnom Penh for 2006 and conducted the establishment survey in Phnom Penh for 2007. The nation-wide establishment listing was made for 2009. 11 The survey does not cover the establishments classified into (i) agriculture, forestry and fishing, (ii) public administration and defense, (iii) activities of households as employers, (iv) activities of extraterritorial organizations and bodies and (v) mobile establishments such as a bike taxi and a street peddler. 12 Each establishment is also asked about a composition of employment, including self-employed proprietors, unpaid family workers and regular employees. 13 A regulatory framework for commercial enterprises in Cambodia was first established by the 'Law Bearing upon Commercial Regulations and the Commercial Register', which was enacted in 1995 and modified in 1999. Our data show that the informal sector is remarkably large in Cambodia's industrial activities. While the formal sector provides large employment opportunities in manufacturing, the informal sector is prominent in both manufacturing and wholesale/retail industries. Additionally, these industries account for the large share of total industrial activity. The wholesale and retail industries accounted for 33.1% of total employment in nonfarm industries, and the manufacturing industries constituted 31.7%. Thus, the analysis of these industries is critical to understanding agglomeration effects in Cambodia.

Using the EC2011, we construct variables on regional productivity, the density of local employment, an industrial diversity index, and a competition index. More specifically, we estimate regional productivity y s i in two steps, with details of the data construction provided in Supplementary Appendix C1. First, we assume that production function for firm f follows a Cobb-Douglas form, q f ¼ A f K f k L f l , where q f is value added; K f is capital input; L f is labor input, and A f is the efficiency level that is observed by a producer, but not by an econometrician. We estimate a log-linear form of the above production function by OLS for a sample on individual firms in each industry. Based on the OLS estimates, we calculate the log of the residuals as a proxy for total factor productivity, ln TFP f À Á . Second, we compute the regional productivity of firms in region i and sector s 2 Formal; Informal f g separately for each industry:
div.formula: y s i ¼ X f2 is q fis P f2 is q fis ln TFP fis À Á
div.p: where is is the set of firms that belong to region i and sector s. The average productivity across region i and sector s for each industry is approximated by the average of firm-level TFP weighted by the share of its own value added in the total value added. An increase in regional productivity results from an increase in the firmlevel TFP values and an expansion of the market share of more productive firms, i.e., allocative efficiency.

div.head: Data on spatial weight matrix
div.p: A spatial-weighting matrix is designed to capture the degree of connectivity between all pairs of distinct regions, which should approximate the spatial dependence in regional productivity that has been formed in past periods up to the year of our cross-sectional data. To approximate such connectivity, we construct a dataset on the shortest travel time between communes in Cambodia. Shorter travel time from one commune to another commune indicates greater connectivity between these communes, whereas longer travel time suggests weaker connectivity. We compute the travel time for the shortest path among all possible routes between commune pairs, which consists of a 1621 Â 1621 matrix with each element estimated in hours. We employ the Floyd-Warshall algorithm to compute the shortest travel time using data on travel distance and speed between communes. These data are constructed from (i) the Geographic Information System (GIS) shape file on 1, 621 administrative units at the commune level in Cambodia, (ii) the map of the Cambodian road network published by the Cambodian Ministry of Public Works and Transport, (iii) the Japan External Trade Organization (JETRO) survey on ASEAN logistics network map (JETRO, 2009) and (iv) satellite-image data of geographic conditions in each commune. Details of the data construction are given in Supplementary Appendix C2. Note that geographic distances between communes are predetermined. Travel speeds depend crucially on the location of major roads that were historically formed on the basis of Cambodia's geography. These facts support the exogenous assumption of the spatial weighting matrix.foot_10

div.head: Other data sources
div.p: Data on population and households are taken from the Population Census of Cambodia in 1998 and 2008. These datasets contain information on the characteristics of the population and households, including residential location, education, and electricity access. Additionally, geographic data on forest and shrubland are constructed from the satellite land cover images provided by the Land Processes Distributed Active Archive Center, a component of NASA's Earth Observing System Data and Information System. Land cover maps in Cambodia are matched with the GIS shape file of communes to calculate the proportion of land areas classified as forest and shrubland for year 2002.

div.head: Main results
div.p: Table 2 presents the summary statistics of the sample used. The mean and standard deviation of variables are shown separately for the formal and informal sectors in manufacturing and wholesale/retail industries, respectively. Regional productivity in the formal sector is higher than that in the informal sector for manufacturing and wholesale/retail industries, consistent with the prior findings that formal enterprises are more productive than informal enterprises (McKenzie and Seynabou Sakho, 2010;Fajnzylber et al., 2011). The formal sector has the higher local density of employment in similar industries and the smaller number of observations than the informal sector does. This implies that formal firms tend to be located in fewer and denser regions, which are more developed in terms of the population size, industrial diversity and electricity access.

Table 3 reports the main estimation results. In manufacturing, the posterior mean coefficient of employment density is 0.016 and insignificant for the formal sector in column (1). In contrast, the posterior mean coefficient is 0.092 for the informal sector in column (2) and statistically significant at the 1% level because the 99% credible interval of the posterior distribution does not contain zero. In wholesale/retail, the posterior mean coefficient of employment density is 0.039 and insignificant for the formal sector in column (3). The posterior mean coefficient is 0.041 and significant at the 10% level for the informal sector in column (4). These results indicate that the density of local employment has a significantly positive effect on the regional productivity only in the informal sector.

We examine the validity of our instruments to check whether positive localization economies in the informal sector can be interpreted as suggesting a causal relationship. First, the past density of employment has the significantly positive posterior mean coefficients at the 1% level across specifications. The past forest variable has significantly negative posterior mean coefficients at the 1% level for the informal sectors in columns (2), (3) and (4). These results imply that our specifications are not likely to suffer from a weak instrument problem. From an economic point of view, a large concentration of industrial activity is likely to attract a large number of workers, suggesting that the past level of employment density significantly affects the spatial pattern of agglomeration. On the other hand, forest regions are likely to discourage the formation of industrial activity for the high cost of leveling the ground. A geographic barrier to worker settlement also significantly influences agglomeration patterns. Second, we compute the Sargan statistic and p-values based on a 2 distribution to check the empirical validity of exclusion restrictions in the specifications. The p-values of the Sargan statistic are large; for instance, the p-values are 0.119 in column (2) and 0.409 in column (4). We do not find strong evidence to reject the null hypothesis that our instrumental variables do not correlate with an error term in equation (4). Taken together, these statistical tests lend support for the identification assumption of our instruments, thereby suggesting a causal impact of the localized concentration of similar industries for the informal sector. We turn to discuss the spatial lag in our model. In manufacturing, the posterior mean coefficient of the spatial lag of productivity is not significant for the formal sector in column (1), but significantly positive at the 1% level for the informal sector in column (2). In wholesale/retail, the posterior mean coefficient for the spatial lag is not significant for the formal sector in column (3), but significantly positive at the 1% level for the informal sector in column (4). These results suggest that there is not significant spatial interdependence of economic performance among formal firms. Meanwhile, informal firms exhibit the positive spatial interdependence among them, implying that the local impact of positive localization economies should be magnified by the positive spatial network within the informal sector. Thus, we find that it is crucial to control for the spatial lag of regional productivity in estimating agglomeration economies in the informal sector.

To further assess a fit of our model with the data, we compute a deviance information criterion (DIC), with a smaller value indicating a better fit of the model (Speigelhalter et al., 2002). Specifically, we compare model fits by computing the DIC for our spatialautoregressive model with a spatial lag variable and a nonspatial autoregressive model without the spatial lag. In manufacturing informal firms, the DIC is 5951.2 for the spatial model and 5993.4 for the non-spatial model, suggesting a better fit of the spatial model. In wholesale/retail informal firms, the DIC is 3782.8 for the spatial model and 3811.2 for the non-spatial model, implying a better fit of the spatial model. These results support that our spatial autoregressive model describes the data in the informal sector better than an alternative model without a spatial lag variable.

To examine the magnitude of localization economies, we compute marginal effects of employment density on regional productivity in the informal sector for manufacturing and wholesale/retail industries. Table 4 presents a summary of average impacts on productivity, which are computed from the results in Table 3. In manufacturing industry, the average direct and indirect impacts are 0.09 and 0.19, respectively. Combining these impacts, we find the average total impact of 0.28. Intuitively, these results indicate that a doubling of the density of local employment increases informal firms' productivity by 9% through direct linkages in their own region and by 19% through spatial multiplier linkages in other regions. These linkages combine to produce a 28% increase in productivity. Additionally, the average direct and indirect impacts in wholesale/retail are 0.04 and 0.17, respectively. The average total impact is 0.21. Intuitively, a doubling of the density of local employment increases the productivity of informal firms by 4% through direct linkages in their own region and by 17% through spatial multiplier linkages, which combine to produce a 21% increase in productivity. Thus, the average indirect impact is larger than the average direct impact in both industries. These results suggest that informal firms benefit significantly from the local impact of localization economies, and consequently the spatial network structure contributes to magnify the localization economies through spatial multiplier linkages. The spatial dependence in economic performance plays a crucial role in estimating the precise magnitude of localization economies.foot_11

div.head: Robustness checks
div.p: In the benchmark analysis, we measure industrial agglomeration by the density of workers. Henderson (2003) and Martin et al. (2011) argue that localization economies can be examined by using the number of firms in the same industry and region. If agglomeration externalities occur mainly through an interaction within firms rather than within workers, we might underestimate the localization economies in the benchmark results. To address this concern, we extend the main specification by measuring the agglomeration as the density of firms in the same industry and commune.

Table 5 presents the estimation results. In manufacturing, the posterior mean coefficient of firm density is 0.015 and insignificant for the formal sector in column (1). The coefficient is 0.102 and significant at the 1% level for the informal sector in column (2). In wholesale/retail, the posterior mean coefficient of firm density is 0.038 and insignificant for the formal sector in column (3). The coefficient is 0.041 and significant at the 10% level for the informal sector in column (4). In columns ( 2) and ( 4), the posterior mean coefficients of past employment density and past forest are significantly positive at the 1% level. The Sargan statistic has a large p-value in these specifications. These results support the validity of our instrumental variables in the specification using the density of firms. Thus, the density of firms also has a positive impact on regional productivity in the informal sector across industries, and the magnitude of the posterior mean coefficient is similar to the results using employment density. The benchmark results are robust to the alternative definition of industrial agglomeration.

For further robustness checks, we estimate the benchmark specification with additional control variables. 17 In the first specification, we include cropland area to capture the effect of agriculture on industrial location and a dummy variable for border regions to account for an accessibility advantage in exporting to foreign markets through land borders. We also include a dummy variable for major international airports and special economic zones. In the second specification, we include the spatial lag of the density of local employment to address a possible confounding factor due to a spatial concentration of similar industries in other regions. We find that the estimation results in these alternative specifications do not differ substantially from the main estimation results, supporting the positive localization economies in the informal sector.

div.head: Further issues
div.p: Previous discussions up to this point suggest that the density of local employment in similar industries has a positive impact on regional productivity in the informal sector, but has little influence in the formal sector. These findings raise further questions. First, we have focused on the density of total employment in both formal and informal sectors to investigate the average cluster benefit. It is plausible that formal firms benefit strongly from a localized cluster of formal firms and weakly from that of informal firms, suggesting that our measure might lead to insignificant localization economies for the formal sector. On the other hand, informal firms may also benefit strongly (weakly) from a localized cluster of informal (formal) firms. The previous results may mask heterogeneous localization economies in terms of the proportion of formal firms in a cluster.

To address this issue, we extend the benchmark specification with an interaction term between the density of employment and the proportion of formal-firm employment in similar industries across regions. Table 6 presents the estimation results. In manufacturing, the posterior mean coefficient of employment density remains insignificant for the formal sector in column (1). The posterior mean coefficient of the interaction term is À0.135 and the 95% credible interval of the posterior distribution does not contain zero. A large proportion of formal firms reduces positive localization impacts for the formal sector, possibly suggesting that a localized concentration of formal manufacturing firms significantly raises congestion costs. Additionally, the posterior mean coefficients of employment density and the interaction are 0.107 and À0.154 for the informal sector in column (2), respectively. The 99% credible intervals of their posterior distributions do not contain zero. Consistent with the result in column (1), a large share of formal firms decreases positive localization effects for the informal sector. In other words, a large proportion of informal firms in a cluster can magnify positive localization effects for the informal sector. Finally, the results for wholesale/ 2) and those in wholesale/retail for columns (3) and (4); formal share shows the share of employment by registered firms in the same industry across regions.

Agglomeration economies . 61 retail industry show that the posterior mean coefficients of the interaction are insignificant for both formal and informal sectors in columns (3) and ( 4). Finally, we discuss whether denser local employment always increases positive localization effects. Because more clustering would increase not only localization benefits but congestion costs, congestion costs may exceed positive localization externalities in high clustering regions. Thus, there may be a nonlinear relationship between clustering and productivity. The estimation results are explained in Supplementary Appendix D. Additionally, informal firms and workers are heterogeneous in many respects such as the degree of informality (Mazumbar, 1976). To shed light on heterogeneity in the informal sector, Supplementary Appendix D reports results for alternative classifications of informal unregistered firms in manufacturing.

div.head: Concluding remarks
div.p: It is widely held that industrial clusters produce agglomeration economies and promote industrialization in developing economies, as has been previously demonstrated for high and middle income countries. However, the large informal sector in developing economies poses a question as to whether both formal and informal firms would benefit from industrial clusters. Using a comprehensive dataset on formally registered and unregistered business establishments in Cambodia, this article estimates the long-run magnitude of agglomeration economies produced by a localized concentration of similar industries. We develop a Bayesian spatial approach to address the endogeneity of industrial agglomeration and spatial dependence in economic performance.

We find that localization economies are significantly positive in the informal sector, but have little effect on the formal sector. In manufacturing, a doubling of employment density increases regional productivity in the informal sector by 9% through local linkages and by 19% through spatial multiplier linkages, leading to a 28% increase in total. Similar results are found for wholesale/retail industry. A spatial network serves to magnify the positive impact of localization economies in the informal sector.

These results provide policy implications for developing economies. The low level of cluster benefits in the formal sector may indicate the weak linkages between formal and informal firms. To produce agglomeration economies for the formal sector, it would be necessary to promote the entry and growth of formal firms such as foreign-owned firms. On the other hand, the informal sector contributes to agglomeration economies, and thus it is not justified to encourage excessively the formalization of informal firms. Additionally, the spatial network among firms can magnify agglomeration economies through geographic connectivity. Because an improvement in transportation infrastructure can enhance agglomeration economies, investment in such infrastructures should be made to reduce congestion costs in excessively dense regions and to improve connectivity between dense regions.

The values of the other prior parameters are assumed as follows: Specifying prior parameters is difficult when no information is available for unknown parameters. Following the standard practice in Bayesian estimation, we choose zero values for the location parameters of the prior distributions for the coefficients. This assumption implies that our prior beliefs for the coefficients are centered on zero. Based on these zero values, we investigate the extent to which the posterior distributions move away from the prior distributions. We set these priors to have large variances to ensure that our prior beliefs for the unknown parameters are non-informative.

Based on the likelihood and the prior for our model, we draw a posterior inference based on the Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method. This method allows us to generate samples from the posteriors and to draw a statistical inference using the simulated samples. Bayesian inference is based on the posterior distributions of unknown parameters. Details of the MCMC sampling are given in Supplementary Appendix B. Additionally, we conduct Monte Carlo simulation to investigate the estimation performance of our model, with details given in Supplementary Appendix B.

Finally, we highlight the advantage of our approach over the prior approach in estimating a spatial autoregressive model with an endogenous independent variable. Kelejian and Prucha (1998) propose higher order spatial lags of exogenous independent variables as instruments for the spatial lag of a dependent variable. This method is applied by Artis et al. (2012) in estimating agglomeration economies. However, Gibbons and Overman (2012) argue that this approach suffers from estimation problems for identification. Specifically, it is assumed that the higher order spatial lags do not affect the dependent variable directly. If this exclusion restriction is not valid, the instruments are not appropriate. Moreover, these instruments may be weak because of potentially high correlations among the higher order spatial lags. In this case, it leads to a biased estimate for the spatial lag variable. In contrast, our Bayesian approach does not exploit higher order spatial lags as instruments, thereby relaxing the identification assumptions used in the prior method. By controlling for potential spatial autocorrelation in the dependent variable, we can focus on the identification of the endogenous independent variable in the spatial autoregressive model.
